title: Psalm 86: Give Me an Undivided Heart
summary: In a time of distress, with arrogant and ruthless men seeking his life, David calls on the Lord as a poor and needy servant who trusts him. He grounds his plea in God's character: kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion, unlike any of the gods, the one before whom all nations will bow. He asks God to teach him his way and unite his heart, and he closes with a request for a sign of God's goodness.
story: Psalm 86 is the only psalm in Book III (Psalms 73 to 89) that carries David's name. It stands in the middle of the Korahite psalms (84, 85, 87, 88), like a personal prayer set between communal songs. Book III is dominated by national crisis, and it will end with the lament of Psalm 89 over God's apparent rejection of David's line. Placing a prayer of David here gives the reader a picture of the kind of king God's covenant had in view: not a proud ruler but a servant who calls himself poor and needy and depends entirely on God's mercy. The psalm's confidence that all nations will one day come and worship the LORD (verse 9) widens the horizon beyond Israel's troubles to the purpose God has for the whole world.
historical: The heading calls the psalm "A prayer of David", a label shared only with Psalms 17 and 142 among the Psalms (Psalm 72 ends with a note that the prayers of David son of Jesse are completed). Whether the headings record authorship or later editorial judgment is debated. Readers who take the heading as authorial note that the psalm's situation, a man hunted by a band of violent enemies, fits more than one period of David's life, including his flight from Saul and the rebellion of Absalom. Many critical scholars regard the psalm as later, pointing out that it is woven almost entirely from phrases found elsewhere in Scripture: verse 1 echoes other laments of David, verse 8 echoes the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:11), verse 14 closely parallels Psalm 54:3, and verse 15 quotes God's self-description to Moses in Exodus 34:6. On that view the psalm was composed by someone steeped in Israel's earlier prayers and placed under David's name as the model of the praying king. Neither view changes what the psalm teaches, and no event is named in the text.
cultural:
Two social pictures run through the psalm. The first is the servant and master. David calls himself God's servant three times and, in verse 16, "the son of Your maidservant". In the ancient world a slave born into a household (the child of a household servant) belonged to that house from birth and had a claim on the master's protection that a hired worker did not. The phrase is a plea for belonging: I have always been yours.

The second is the ancient belief in many gods. Every nation around Israel had its own deities, and victories in war were often credited to them. When the psalmist says "there is none like You among the gods" (verse 8), he is taking up the language of that world in order to deny that any other power compares with the LORD. Verse 10 then says it plainly: "You alone are God." Sheol (verse 13) was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a place deep beneath the earth; to be delivered from its depths meant being rescued from a threat of death.
literary: Psalm 86 is an individual lament, a personal prayer in distress. It is built around a center of praise. Verses 1 to 7 are a string of short petitions (incline, answer, preserve, save, be merciful, bring joy, hear), each backed by a reason introduced by "for" or "because". Verses 8 to 13 turn to praise and to the central request: "Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart" (verse 11). Verses 14 to 17 return to lament and petition, now naming the enemies and quoting Exodus 34:6. The title Adonai, Lord, appears seven times, far more than usual in a single psalm, and it is the address of a servant to a master. Much of the psalm's language is borrowed from other Scripture, which is not a weakness: it shows a person learning to pray by praying words God's people had already prayed.

outline.t: Petitions of a poor and needy servant
None like you: the nations will bow
Teach me your way and unite my heart
Ruthless enemies and a compassionate God

doctrines.note: Verse 15 repeats the heart of God's self-revelation at Sinai: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness. The whole prayer rests on who God has said he is.
The psalm models prayer that gives reasons: I am needy, I trust you, you are forgiving, you answer. It also asks not only for rescue but for inner change, a heart taught and made whole.
Even in personal distress the psalmist remembers that "All the nations You have made will come and bow before You" (verse 9). God's care for one servant belongs to his purpose for all peoples.

words.note: Yachad, to be joined or united. In verse 11 the psalmist asks God to unite his heart, which the BSB renders "Give me an undivided heart". A divided heart is pulled between fear of God and other loyalties; a united one is whole in its devotion. The request recognizes that even wholehearted fear of God is something God must give.

Chasid, godly or faithful. The word is related to chesed, God's covenant love, and describes a person who is loyal within that covenant. When the psalmist says "I am godly" (verse 2), he is claiming to belong to God's faithful people, not to be sinless.

Rachum, compassionate. The word is related to the Hebrew for womb, and it describes a tender, motherly kind of mercy. It stands first in the list of God's attributes in verse 15, quoted from Exodus 34:6.
Adonai, Lord or Master. It appears seven times in this psalm. It is the title a servant uses of a master, and it matches the psalmist's repeated description of himself as God's servant.

christ: Verse 9 looks forward to the day when the nations God made will come and bow before him and glorify his name. The book of Revelation echoes this psalm in the song of those who have conquered: all nations will come and worship before God (Revelation 15:4). Paul describes the same worship gathered around Jesus, at whose name every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10-11). The link is a fulfillment of the psalm's hope rather than a hidden prediction. The psalm's portrait of the king as a poor and needy servant, surrounded by ruthless men and trusting God to vindicate him, also anticipates the one the New Testament calls the Son of David, who took the form of a servant and prayed in his own distress to the God who is compassionate and gracious.

hard.q: How can the psalmist say "I am godly" without sounding self-righteous?
hard.a:
Modern readers often hear verse 2 as a boast, but the Hebrew word (chasid) describes loyalty within a relationship, not moral perfection. The psalmist is saying that he belongs to God and has not abandoned him, which is why he can appeal to God's protection. The rest of the psalm makes his posture clear: he calls himself poor and needy, pleads for mercy, praises God as forgiving, and asks to be taught. Other psalms make similar claims of integrity in the same spirit (Psalm 26:1, for example).

Interpreters differ slightly in emphasis. Some stress that the claim is covenantal: God has bound himself to his faithful ones, and the psalmist asks him to keep his word. Others stress that such claims are relative to the charges of enemies: the psalmist is innocent of what his persecutors accuse him of. Either way, the claim sits comfortably beside dependence on grace, which is the note the psalm sounds most often.

questions: The psalmist asks God to unite his heart. What loyalties or fears pull your heart in different directions?
Much of this psalm is built from earlier Scripture. How might praying the Bible's own words shape the way you pray?
Verse 15 describes God as compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in love. Which of these do you find hardest to believe about God, and why?
